summary.en: Serious lyrics and music, plus instrumental virtuosity and new technology, made rock begin to take itself seriously—perhaps the start of the hippie aesthetic.
summary.zh: 严肃的歌词与音乐，加之演奏乐器的精湛技巧和对新技术的使用，使得摇滚乐开始变得严肃起来，这或许就是嬉皮美学的开端。

body.zh:
严肃的歌词与音乐，加之演奏乐器的精湛技巧和对新技术的使用，使得摇滚乐开始变得严肃起来，这或许就是嬉皮美学的开端。

上节课我们讲到了LSD的风行。很重要的一点是，LSD并非只在67、68、69年从亚文化群体到主流文化中被单纯当作致幻药物使用，它还被用来创造一种“神游”的体验。很多音乐家创造出了配合神游体验的音乐，可以增强体验效果；或者创作出能够让人获得神游体验的歌曲。不使用LSD，光听专辑就能进行神游，这有可能吗？我们要谈谈摇滚乐如何开始严肃地对待这个挑战，即“创造足以带给人神游体验的音乐”。这是一个新概念的起源，我们在《摇滚史》的第二部分会讲到，我称之为嬉皮美学（Hippie Aesthetic）。

是什么构成了音乐的嬉皮美学呢？这种音乐上的雄心可以追溯到1959年The Drifters的《There Goes My Baby》，制作人是Lieber and Stoller。歌曲中管弦乐的应用不仅限于营造甜美感，他们犹如古典乐般的弦乐编配真的很抢眼。我们可以想想Phil Spector的野心，用音墙创造最大声效的想法就有点像青年交响乐团的感觉。Brian Wilson不再跟The Beach Boys巡演后进行的录音室实验，将录音室作为构图画板，描绘出新的声音，其音乐越来越有雄心。The Beatles也越来越严肃，我们在讨论英伦入侵时，循迹了The Beatles从匠人到艺术家的发展历程。Bob Dylan和他那些严肃的歌词在60年代中期浮出台面。从66、67年开始，音乐家们开始思考如何严肃地对待音乐，他们在一定程度上进行了各种尝试，以期增加音乐的严肃性。

我们先来讨论一下严肃的歌词（Serious Lyrics）。嬉皮美学与许多迷幻音乐的一个特点是，歌词的主题是严肃的，不仅仅是青春年华、爱情故事、“我想要牵你的手”、“她爱你”等等，还有一些严肃的话题，关于精神层面、社会、战争的恐怖等。当然在某种程度上，Dylan用自己的歌词为这些严肃的话题铺了路，同时也展示了歌词本身的精雕细琢。这跟概念专辑的发展是密不可分的，专辑作为整体时，意义应该比单看每首歌更大，专辑本身由一个概念贯穿，专辑的包装也占有一席之地。这样的专辑歌词严肃，围绕着一个中心思想，专辑的艺术表达也参与其中，变得比之前更有雄心。

严肃的音乐（Serious Music）是另一种增加严肃性的方法，即向那些已经十分严肃的音乐风格靠拢，被借鉴最广泛的两种音乐形式是古典乐与爵士乐。就古典乐而言，摇滚乐常向两种古典乐靠拢，一种是19世纪的传统古典音乐，即今天的古典音乐电台播放的那种，管弦乐、弦乐四重奏之类的，勃拉姆斯、贝多芬、海顿、莫扎特、肖邦等精心制作的钢琴作品，甚至20世纪的拉赫玛尼诺夫，这些极具调性的古典音乐。另一种则是先锋音乐 (Avant-garde) ，如磁带音乐、合成器，各种疯狂、创新的东西，60年代的典型是卡尔海因茨·施托克豪森。就爵士乐而言，主要是调式爵士（Modal Jazz）对摇滚产生了影响，以及Miles Davis在50年代末的《Kind of Blue》，接着是John Coltrane和其他身处同一浪潮的音乐人。上述的古典乐及爵士乐，都是有庞大群体的严肃音乐类型，如果在摇滚中引入这些元素，音乐就会变得更严肃。

同时，人们开始关注精湛技巧（Virtuosity）。之后我们会再讲到摇滚中技巧的发展，Jimmy Hendrix、Eric Clapton等吉他英雄的发展。此时，精于乐器变得有意义了。你不再只是站在那儿，衣着光鲜亮丽，帮主唱伴奏。你开始精进技巧，无论是吉他、键盘、鼓还是贝斯，技巧开始变得重要。要么是古典乐的技巧，要么是爵士乐的技巧，Itzhak Perlman、John Coltrane，还是Charlie Parker、Miles Davis，谁是你的技巧派偶像？

技术（Technology）的使用是增进音乐严肃性的另一个方法。比如，追求先进的录音技术，能够将更多的音轨放进一首歌中，也能在录音室里用各种方法控制声音。比如我们之前提到的Brian Wilson，录音棚开始变成构筑创意的画板，在60年代末期，这开始变成一种标准。本课程第二部分会讲到，在70年代它变得非常重要。在68年晚期到69年，出现了第一个使用合成器的例子，主要是Moog合成器。但在初期 Moog合成器还上不了台，因为它十分巨大，需要用整间房来装它。又大又复杂，难以操作，需要一个人来专门操作它。而第一个采样合成器，是我们提到过的Mellotron，在The Beatles的歌曲《Strawberry Fields Forever》中出现过。它的每个键都会触发不同的录音，可能是管弦乐、合唱团或长笛演奏某个音。当你同时按下管弦乐团演奏的C、E跟G的键时，就产生了管弦乐团在演奏的效果。最早的采样器即模拟采样器，一出现便走入了所有人的音乐中，因为它非常新颖，从来没人听过这样的效果。作为一个有雄心的乐手，你会去创作新的东西，以前从未有过的、实验性的，或许是迷幻风格的东西。

最重要的是“摇滚乐手是艺术家”这样的想法开始成形。不仅是有着漂亮脸蛋、上Ed Sullivan Show的娱乐演员，而是需要发展与保护自己的艺术主张，以期在业界中获得声誉的人。勇于探索新的可能性，拓展音乐的边界。把所有这些歌词、音乐、技巧、技术等综合起来，作为一个艺术家，对自己的音乐负责。这样的想法，从50年代末一路发展过来，到66、67、68、69年，这开始变成主流模式。主要因为音乐人在寻找一种让自己的音乐更严肃的方法，想要让音乐的分量更重一些。一定程度上，这是在追随“神游”这个概念，这或许是音乐开始变得迷幻的原因。在探讨音乐本身之前，我们先来探讨一下The Beatles与The Beach Boys的创新，让我们更深层地理解到音乐如何变得迷幻。
body.en:
Serious lyrics and music, plus instrumental virtuosity and new technology, made rock begin to take itself seriously—perhaps the start of the hippie aesthetic.

Last time we covered LSD’s spread. An important point: LSD was not only a recreational hallucinogen moving from subculture into the mainstream in 1967–69; it was also used to create a “trip” experience. Many musicians made music to accompany trips and heighten them, or songs that could themselves deliver a trip. Could you trip just by listening to an album, without LSD? We will talk about how rock began to take seriously the challenge of “making music that can give a trip.” That is the origin of a new idea we will cover in Part Two of History of Rock—what I call the Hippie Aesthetic.

What makes up the musical hippie aesthetic? This musical ambition can be traced to the Drifters’ 1959 “There Goes My Baby,” produced by Leiber and Stoller. Orchestral writing there was not only for sweetness; the classical-like string arrangement really stands out. Think of Phil Spector’s ambition—the Wall of Sound seeking maximum sonic impact, a bit like a youth orchestra. Brian Wilson’s studio experiments after he stopped touring with the Beach Boys treated the studio as a canvas for new sounds; his music grew more ambitious. The Beatles grew more serious too; when we covered the British Invasion we traced their path from craftsmen to artists. Bob Dylan and his serious lyrics surfaced in the mid-1960s. From 1966–67 on, musicians asked how to treat music seriously and tried various ways to add weight.

Start with serious lyrics. A trait of the hippie aesthetic and much psychedelic music is serious subject matter—not only youth, love stories, “I Want to Hold Your Hand,” “She Loves You,” but spiritual themes, society, the horror of war. Dylan, to a degree, paved the way with such lyrics and showed how carefully words could be crafted. That is inseparable from the concept album: as a whole an album should mean more than each song alone; one concept runs through it, and packaging matters. Such albums have serious lyrics around a central idea, and the album’s art joins in—more ambitious than before.

Serious music is another path: leaning toward styles already treated as serious. The two most borrowed forms are classical and jazz. In classical, rock often approaches two kinds: nineteenth-century traditional classical—what classical radio plays today, orchestras, string quartets, carefully made piano works by Brahms, Beethoven, Haydn, Mozart, Chopin, even twentieth-century Rachmaninoff—strongly tonal music; and avant-garde—tape music, synthesizers, wild innovative work, with Karlheinz Stockhausen typical of the 1960s. In jazz, modal jazz especially shaped rock, plus Miles Davis’s late-1950s Kind of Blue, then John Coltrane and others in that wave. Those classical and jazz worlds already had large serious audiences; importing their elements made rock feel more serious.

People also began to care about virtuosity. We will return to technique in rock—guitar heroes such as Jimi Hendrix and Eric Clapton. Skill on an instrument started to matter. You were no longer just standing there looking sharp, backing the singer. You refined technique on guitar, keyboards, drums, or bass. Classical technique or jazz technique—Itzhak Perlman, John Coltrane, Charlie Parker, Miles Davis: who was your virtuoso idol?

Technology was another way to heighten seriousness: advanced recording that could put more tracks into a song and control sound in the studio. As with Brian Wilson earlier, the studio became a creative canvas; by the late 1960s that became a standard. In Part Two we will see how important it became in the 1970s. In late 1968–69 the first synthesizer uses appear, mainly Moog—but early Moogs were huge, needing a whole room, hard to operate, requiring a dedicated operator. The first sampling synthesizer we mentioned was the Mellotron, heard on the Beatles’ “Strawberry Fields Forever.” Each key triggered a different recording—orchestra, choir, or flute on a given pitch. Press C, E, and G of orchestral samples together and you get an orchestra playing that chord. Early analog samplers walked into everyone’s music because the sound was brand new. An ambitious player would make something never heard before—experimental, perhaps psychedelic.

Most important, the idea that rock musicians are artists took shape—not just pretty faces on the Ed Sullivan Show, but people who develop and protect an artistic stance and seek standing in the field. Explore new possibilities; push music’s borders. Bring lyrics, music, technique, and technology together; as an artist, take responsibility for your music. That idea grew from the late 1950s; by 1966–69 it was becoming mainstream. Musicians were looking for ways to make music more serious and weightier. To a degree they were chasing the idea of the “trip”—perhaps why music began to sound psychedelic. Before we dig into the music itself, we look at innovations by the Beatles and the Beach Boys, to understand more deeply how music became psychedelic.
